Conclusion: In healthy adults, long-term creatine supplementation at standard doses appears safe for kidney function, although it can modestly raise serum creatinine without indicating actual kidney injury.

References (with the underlying study of each):
[1] 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis of creatine and renal function (J Ren Nutr; the report labels it Antonio et al. 2019, but this journal paper appears to be de Souza e Silva et al. 2019). Underlying study: S1
[2] 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of creatine supplementation and kidney function. Underlying study: S2
[3] Kreider et al. 2003 study of long-term (up to 21 months) creatine use in athletes, as reported in a 2023 narrative review (Requiem review). Underlying study: S3
[4] 2025 short narrative safety review of creatine supplementation. Underlying study: S4
[5] ISSN 2017 position stand on creatine (Kreider et al. 2017). Underlying study: S5

Lines of reasoning:
Line 1: uses references [1]; assumes A1.S1, A10.S1, A5.S1, A8, A9.
Line 2: uses references [2]; assumes A10.S2, A2.S2, A3.S2, A8, A9.

Assumptions:
A1.S1: The participants in the studies pooled by the 2019 meta-analysis are healthy adults using standard doses, matching the population and doses in the conclusion. (for study S1)
A2.S2: The kidney outcomes measured in the 2025 meta-analysis (GFR) are not distorted by the creatine-induced rise in creatinine, for example because GFR was measured or estimated by methods other than serum creatinine, so that 'no adverse GFR effect' reflects real kidney function. (for study S2)
A3.S2: The participants in the 2025 meta-analysis are healthy adults on standard protocols, matching the conclusion population and doses. (for study S2)
A4.S3: The athletes in the 21-month comparison study are representative of healthy adults generally. (for study S3)
A5.S1: The kidney-function markers used (serum and urinary creatinine, urea, eGFR, proteinuria, albuminuria) are sensitive enough to detect clinically relevant renal harm. (for study S1)
A5.S3: The kidney-function markers used (serum and urinary creatinine, urea, eGFR, proteinuria, albuminuria) are sensitive enough to detect clinically relevant renal harm. (for study S3)

A5.S5: The kidney-function markers used (serum and urinary creatinine, urea, eGFR, proteinuria, albuminuria) are sensitive enough to detect clinically relevant renal harm. (for study S5)
A6.S4: The protocols covered by the 2025 safety review include standard doses (3–5 g/day) in healthy adults, so its null findings apply to the conclusion's setting. (for study S4)
A7: The ISSN statement that there is 'no compelling evidence' of kidney dysfunction amounts to positive evidence of safety, not merely an absence of studies.
A8: The creatine-induced rise in serum creatinine comes from creatine-to-creatinine conversion and not from reduced filtration.
A9: Absence of renal harm over the study durations (at most about 5 years, mostly far shorter) holds for the longer-term use intended by the conclusion.
A10.S1: The creatine products and forms tested (mainly creatine monohydrate) match the products consumers actually use. (for study S1)
A10.S2: The creatine products and forms tested (mainly creatine monohydrate) match the products consumers actually use. (for study S2)
A10.S3: The creatine products and forms tested (mainly creatine monohydrate) match the products consumers actually use. (for study S3)

A10.S5: The creatine products and forms tested (mainly creatine monohydrate) match the products consumers actually use. (for study S5)

Conclusion: Long-term creatine supplementation is safe for kidney function in healthy adults when used at standard doses.

Conclusion: In adults, intermittent fasting does not consistently produce more weight loss than continuous calorie restriction; with comparable energy intake both give similar weight loss, though alternate-day fasting may offer a small additional short-term advantage.

References (with the underlying study of each):
[1] BMJ 2025 systematic review and network meta-analysis of 99 RCTs (6,582 adults). Underlying study: S1
[2] Obesity 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 RCTs (623 participants) comparing fasting with continuous caloric restriction. Underlying study: S2
[3] Allaf et al. 2021 Cochrane review on intermittent fasting for cardiovascular disease prevention. Underlying study: S3
[4] 2018 meta-analysis of intermittent vs continuous energy restriction (pooled difference −0.61 kg); the URL points to Journal of Translational Medicine, not BMC Endocrine Disorders. Underlying study: S4
[5] IJBNPA 2024 network meta-analysis of 47 RCTs comparing caloric restriction regimens. Underlying study: S5

Conclusion: In adults, intermittent fasting generally produces weight loss similar to continuous calorie restriction when energy intake is comparable, rather than reliably greater weight loss, although alternate-day fasting may offer a small short-term advantage.

Conclusion: Domestic heat pumps generally reduce heating-related CO₂ emissions compared with gas boilers in the UK, though the size of the reduction depends on heat-pump type, seasonal efficiency, grid carbon intensity, refrigerant impacts and lifecycle scope.

A2.S2: The supplementation regimens, baseline vitamin D distributions, and settings represented in the 43-trial meta-analysis adequately inform population-wide supplementation in adults. (for study S2)
A3.S3: The populations included in the 46-trial meta-analysis permit its overall findings to inform prevention in adults, rather than being driven by results in children or other populations that differ materially from adults generally. (for study S3)
A4.S3: The supplementation regimens, baseline vitamin D distributions, and settings represented in the 46-trial meta-analysis adequately inform population-wide supplementation in adults. (for study S3)
A5.S2: The measured ARI outcomes are sufficiently comparable to whether adults experience an infection; findings about incidence are not being transferred to severity, duration, hospitalization, or mortality. (for study S2)
A5.S3: The measured ARI outcomes are sufficiently comparable to whether adults experience an infection; findings about incidence are not being transferred to severity, duration, hospitalization, or mortality. (for study S3)
A6: The near-null pooled results and their uncertainty justify withholding a claim of dependable population-wide prevention, without requiring that every subgroup or regimen have exactly zero benefit.
A7.S2: Bias in the included trials, selective reporting, and errors in evidence synthesis are not large enough to overturn the interpretation of the cited pooled results. (for study S2)
A7.S3: Bias in the included trials, selective reporting, and errors in evidence synthesis are not large enough to overturn the interpretation of the cited pooled results. (for study S3)
